slides.title: Markov Decision Processes, Policies, and Value Iteration
slides.text: DRIVING PROBLEM Prediction tells us what may happen. An MDP asks what we should do. We begin with Markov-chain foundations, clarify two claims in context, and then add the decision layer from the course textbooks. Model state, action, transition, reward, discount Evaluate policy, return, value, Bellman expectation Optimize Bellman optimality, value iteration, policy extraction Audit state sufficiency, reward design, model error

slides.title: Sequence models connect observations across time or space
slides.text: ORIGINAL KNOWLEDGE POINT Reason about a sequence of observations Introduce time—or space—because the current observation alone may not identify the underlying state. Speech recognition State: phoneme or word position Observation: acoustic frames Robot localization State: location and heading Observation: sensor readings User attention State: attention state Observation: clicks and gaze Medical monitoring State: patient condition Observation: vital signs RETRIEVAL PROMPT For robot localization, what must the state preserve so the next-step distribution no longer needs the entire path history?

slides.title: A Markov model starts with state, an initial distribution, and transitions
slides.text: STATE SEQUENCE X₁ → X₂ → X₃ → X₄ → … P(X₁) P(Xₜ | Xₜ₋₁) State Xₜ The value of X at time t. Initial distribution P(X₁) Uncertainty before the sequence begins. Transition dynamics P(Xₜ|Xₜ₋₁) How the state evolves one step. TERMINOLOGY CORRECTION Reusing the same transition probabilities at every time is a time-homogeneous transition assumption. It is not required by every Markov model and is not the same as a stationary state distribution.

slides.title: The Markov assumption shortens the chain-rule history
slides.text: X₁ → X₂ → X₃ → X₄ → … 1 · CHAIN RULE IDENTITY P(x₁:ₜ) = P(x₁) ∏i=2T P(xᵢ | x₁:ᵢ₋₁) Valid for every joint distribution. 2 · FIRST-ORDER ASSUMPTION Xᵢ ⟂ X₁:ᵢ₋₂ | Xᵢ₋₁ The present state screens off earlier history. 3 · MARKOV FACTORIZATION P(x₁:ₜ) = P(x₁) ∏i=2T P(xᵢ | xᵢ₋₁) A modeling assumption makes the factors local. IN-CLASS CHECK Which line is a probability identity, and which line introduces the Markov modeling assumption?

slides.title: Given the present, earlier history adds no information about the next state
slides.text: EXPLICIT ASSUMPTION Xₜ ⟂ X₁:ₜ₋₂ | Xₜ₋₁ Each state needs only the previous state. IMPLIED PROPERTY past ⟂ future | present Knowing the present blocks information flow along the chain. PROOF IDEA factor, cancel, normalize For example, P(X₁|X₂,X₃,X₄)=P(X₁|X₂). CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL WORDING Past and future are conditionally independent given the present; they are not “independent of the present.”

slides.title: An unrolled first-order chain is a Bayesian network
slides.text: X₁ → X₂ → X₃ → X₄ → … GRAPH FORM A growable Bayesian network Truncate at horizon T to obtain a finite directed acyclic graph. PROBABILITY FORM Multiply local factors P(x₁)P(x₂|x₁)…P(xₜ|xₜ₋₁). INDEPENDENCE FORM Condition on an intermediate state X₁ and X₄ may be dependent marginally, but are independent given X₂ or X₃.

slides.title: One transition model has three equivalent representations
slides.text: CPT current next P sun sun .9 sun rain .1 rain sun .3 rain rain .7 STATE GRAPH sun .9 loop · .1 → rain rain .7 loop · .3 → sun MATRIX T = [ .9 .1 .3 .7 ] Rows: current state; columns: next state. REPRESENTATION CHECK Map one CPT row to the matching outgoing graph edges and matrix row. Each row must sum to 1.

slides.title: From all sun, one step produces 0.9 sun and 0.1 rain
slides.text: GIVEN P₁(sun)=1.0 · P₁(rain)=0.0 LAW OF TOTAL PROBABILITY P₂(sun) = P(sun|sun)P₁(sun) + P(sun|rain)P₁(rain) = 0.9(1.0) + 0.3(0.0) = 0.9 P₂(rain) = 0.1(1.0) + 0.7(0.0) = 0.1 PREDICT BEFORE REVEALING Why must both next-state probabilities add to 1?

slides.title: Forward prediction repeatedly applies the same transition operator
slides.text: FORWARD PREDICTION Pₜ(xₜ)=Σxₜ₋₁P(xₜ|xₜ₋₁)Pₜ₋₁(xₜ₋₁) Prediction only: no observation update. initial belief P(X₁) P(X₂) P(X₃) P(X₄) limit All sun (1.000, 0.000) (0.900, 0.100) (0.840, 0.160) (0.804, 0.196) (.750, .250) All rain (0.000, 1.000) (0.300, 0.700) (0.480, 0.520) (0.588, 0.412) (.750, .250) Any p (p, 1−p) repeated transition updates (.750, .250)

slides.title: A stationary distribution is a fixed point—not a universal convergence promise
slides.text: DEFINITION A stationary distribution π is unchanged by one transition π = πT, or π(x′)=ΣₓP(x′|x)π(x). WEATHER EQUATIONS π(sun)=.9π(sun)+.3π(rain) π(rain)=.1π(sun)+.7π(rain) π(sun)+π(rain)=1 SOLVE π(sun)=¾ π(rain)=¼ CONVERGENCE CONDITION This chain converges because it is finite, irreducible, and aperiodic. A stationary distribution alone does not guarantee convergence from every start.

slides.title: A Markov chain predicts; an MDP adds choices and consequences
slides.text: MARKOV CHAIN Current state → random next state P(s′|s) No decision variable Models how a process evolves Question: what will happen? + DECISION LAYER Choose action a in state s P(s′|s,a) and R(s,a,s′) Policy selects actions Rewards encode the objective Question: what should the agent do?

slides.title: An MDP is the tuple ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩
slides.text: S States Information the model treats as sufficient for predicting the next transition and reward. A Actions Choices available to the agent; A(s) may depend on the state. P Transitions P(s′|s,a), a probability distribution over next states. R Reward R(s,a,s′), the immediate scalar signal used by the objective. γ Discount 0≤γ<1 for continuing discounted tasks; weights later rewards. MARKOV REQUIREMENT Given the modeled state and current action, the distribution of next state and reward must not require additional history. If it does, the state representation is insufficient.

slides.title: Actions change transition distributions; they do not guarantee outcomes
slides.text: EXAMPLE · MOVE RIGHT P(s′|s,Right) 0.80 move right 0.10 slip up 0.10 slip down Walls redirect an attempted move to “stay” in this model. 0.00 S00 0.00 S01 1.00 TERMINAL 0.00 S10 WALL -1.00 TERMINAL 0.00 S20 0.00 S21 0.00 S22 PROBABILITY AUDIT For every state-action pair, Σs′P(s′|s,a)=1. Deterministic dynamics are the special case with one successor at probability 1.

slides.title: Reward is the formal objective—not a label for what humans value
slides.text: GRIDWORLD REWARD MODEL +1 goal · −1 hazard · −0.04 per nonterminal step The living cost favors shorter paths, but it can also change risk preference. A more negative cost may drive the agent near hazards; a positive living reward may encourage endless wandering. Specify Whose outcome is represented? Stress-test Can the objective be gamed? Constrain Which harms are unacceptable regardless of reward? Monitor Does deployment differ from the modeled setting?

slides.title: Return adds immediate and discounted future rewards
slides.text: γ = 0.0 γ = 0.5 γ = 0.9 γ = 1.0 T + 0 r = 5 0.90 × 5 = 5.00 T + 1 r = 0 0.91 × 0 = 0.00 T + 2 r = 8 0.92 × 8 = 6.48 T + 3 r = 2 0.93 × 2 = 1.46 DISCOUNTED RETURN Gt = 12.94 γ controls how quickly later rewards lose weight; it does not express uncertainty and it does not repair a poorly chosen reward.

slides.title: A policy chooses; a value function predicts long-run return
slides.text: POLICY π(a|s) A distribution over actions in each state. Deterministic π(s) is a special case. Question answered: What will the agent choose? STATE VALUE Vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt|St=s] Expected return from state s when policy π is followed. Question answered: How good is this state under π? ACTION VALUE Qπ(s,a)=Eπ[Gt|s,a] Expected return after taking a now and following π afterward. Question answered: How good is this choice?

slides.title: Bellman expectation decomposes value into one step plus the remainder
slides.text: POLICY Π AT STATE S π(right|s)=0.75 · π(left|s)=0.25 Immediate reward is −0.1 and γ=0.9. “Right” reaches a state valued 4 with probability 0.8 and a state valued 2 with probability 0.2. “Left” reaches a state valued 1. Reveal next line Reveal all 1 Predict this line Name the expectation before revealing it. 2 Predict this line Name the expectation before revealing it. 3 Predict this line Name the expectation before revealing it.

slides.title: Policy evaluation averages; optimal control maximizes
slides.text: BELLMAN EXPECTATION Vπ(s)=Σaπ(a|s)Σs′P(s′|s,a)[R+γVπ(s′)] Evaluate a specified policy—even if it sometimes chooses a weaker action. BELLMAN OPTIMALITY V*(s)=maxaΣs′P(s′|s,a)[R+γV*(s′)] Choose the action whose expected one-step backup is largest. CHECK FOR UNDERSTANDING Which change turns Bellman expectation into Bellman optimality? A Replace the successor-state expectation with a maximum B Replace the policy-weighted action average with a maximum C Remove the immediate reward

buttons.text: AReplace the successor-state expectation with a maximum
BReplace the policy-weighted action average with a maximum

slides.title: A Bellman optimality backup compares every action at one state
slides.text: ↑ Up → Right ↓ Down ← Left ONE DETERMINISTIC ACTION BACKUP Q(s,Right) = −0.04 + 0.9(0.7) = 0.59 Successor: bottom-right. CURRENT MAXIMUM Bellman optimality keeps the largest action backup. Here, Vnew(s)=max(0.32, 0.59, 0.32, 0.14)=0.59, so Right is greedy.

slides.title: Value iteration applies Bellman optimality synchronously until change is small
slides.text: Initialize Choose V₀(s), often zero for nonterminals. Back up Vk+1(s) ← maxaΣs′P(s′|s,a)[R+γVk(s′)]. Measure Δ ← maxs|Vk+1(s)−Vk(s)|. Repeat Stop by a justified residual or iteration rule. Extract π(s) ← argmaxa one-step lookahead using final V. SYNCHRONOUS MEANS PREVIOUS SWEEP Every Vk+1(s) uses Vk, not values already updated during the same sweep. In-place variants can work, but they are a different update schedule.

slides.title: Watch value information move through a 3×3 gridworld
slides.text: INTERACTIVE SYNCHRONOUS VALUE ITERATION Sweep 0 · max Δ = 0.0000 Deterministic moves, wall collision means “stay,” living reward −0.04, γ=0.9, terminal values +1 and −1. Every nonterminal cell uses only values from the previous sweep. Previous Run one sweep Run to 30 Show greedy policy OBSERVE THE WAVE Positive terminal value propagates left and downward one sweep at a time. Values are not rewards; they summarize expected discounted future reward under the current greedy backup. 0.00 S00 0.00 S01 1.00 TERMINAL 0.00 S10 WALL -1.00 TERMINAL 0.00 S20 0.00 S21 0.00 S22

slides.title: A small Bellman residual is solver evidence, not real-world validation
slides.text: DISCOUNTED FINITE MDP The Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction With 0≤γ<1 and bounded rewards, repeated optimality backups converge to a unique V*. The residual Δ measures numerical change under the model. Iteration rule Stop after a fixed compute budget; simple, but no direct accuracy guarantee. Residual rule Stop when max state change is below a chosen tolerance. Policy stability Monitor whether greedy actions stop changing; ties need care. DO NOT CONFLATE ERRORS Small iteration error does not imply small transition-model error, reward-specification error, or deployment risk.

slides.title: Once values stabilize, one-step lookahead yields a greedy policy
slides.text: 0.73 → 0.86 → 1.00 TERMINAL 0.62 ↑ WALL -1.00 TERMINAL 0.52 ↑ 0.43 ← 0.34 ← SELECTED STATE · 2-0 Extract π*(s) by taking argmaxa Q(s,a) ↑ Up to 1-0 0.519 ↓ Down to 2-0 0.427 ← Left to 2-0 0.427 → Right to 2-1 0.344 TIE POLICY If multiple actions share the maximum, a deterministic policy may choose any maximizer; a stochastic policy may distribute probability among them.

slides.title: An elegant solution can still optimize the wrong model
slides.text: State Reward Dynamics Planning CLAIM TO AUDIT Location alone is a sufficient state for a delivery robot. Diagnosis Usually incomplete: remaining battery, payload, time, and relevant traffic conditions can change transition or reward predictions. Evidence plan Test whether next-state and reward distributions still depend on omitted history after conditioning on the proposed state.

slides.title: Model the future, choose a policy, and defend the assumptions
slides.text: Represent Write ⟨S,A,P,R,γ⟩ for a two-state decision problem. Calculate Complete one Bellman expectation or optimality backup. Explain Why is an MDP not merely a Markov chain? Audit Name one omitted variable or reward failure and evidence that would reveal it.
